newsitem.title: FRANCE: PRIVATE PENSION FUND BILL CLEARS HURDLES.
newsitem.headline: PRIVATE PENSION FUND BILL CLEARS HURDLES.

text.p: A bill to introduce private pension funds to France passed one of the last outstanding hurdles on Thursday when it was adopted, with some amendents by the Senate after a second reading.

The opposition Socialist Party voted against the proposal and stated their intention to ask the country's Consitutional Council to quash the bill as well as vowing to repeal it if they come to power in the 1998 legislative elections.
The bill is scheduled go to a mixed Senate-National Assembly committee on Feburary 5 for final arbitration on the amendments, the last step before definitive adoption.

The main amendment voted by the Senate aims to reduce the amount a private pension fund can hold in any one company to five percent of the firm's share capital, from the 10 percent ceiling approved in a second reading by the National Assembly.

There was no change to the most controverisal clause, already agreed between the two houses of parliament, which exempts employers from social security charges on contributions they make on behalf on employees.
The Socialists, Communists and all main trade unions say this is an incentive that will deprive the social security system of money used for state-backed retirement benefit.
Another amendement adopted by the upper house would allow employees to subscribe to a pension fund outside their company if the firm has not agreed a collective private pension deal within a year.
The National Assembly envisaged a two-year waiting period.
The Senate also said defined-payout pensions plans should be prohibited, to help promote investment in equities.
The bill, as agreed by both houses of parliament, will cap pension fund investment in fixed-income bonds at 65 percent in an attempt to secure investment in France's weakly capitalised stock market.
